mcqs.question: A support assistant answers 68% of a 200-question eval set correctly. An engineer proposes to fix the rest by tightening the system prompt and lowering temperature, arguing that the wrong answers are 'a generation problem'. The pipeline already logs, for every request, the ids of the chunks that were passed to the model. Which next step actually separates the two layers?
options: Re-run the 64 failing questions twice at temperature 0 and compare the two answers: if the wording moves between runs, generation is the cause, since temperature and instructions are the only things that differ between two identical requests.

For each failing question, check whether the gold chunk was in the retrieved set: absent means the fault is upstream (parse, chunk, embed, filter or rank) where no prompt can recover it; present means the answer ignored or misread the evidence, which is a generation and evidence-format question.

Score each failing answer with an LLM judge on a 1-5 helpfulness scale and bucket the results: the low-scoring half points at generation, the high-scoring half at retrieval, and each bucket then gets its own fix.

Compare answer length against the gold answer and flag the short ones as missing-evidence cases: a short answer means the context was incomplete, a long one means the model over-generated beyond what it was given.
mcqs.explanation: The label has to be per question and it has to say whether the evidence arrived: retrieval is the cheaper layer to falsify, and prompt work on absent evidence is wasted effort, which is the triage order the pipeline itself prescribes - did the right chunk appear in the top-k, and is every claim supported by it (https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/grounding/overview, https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/evals). The strongest distractor is the temperature-0 rerun, because it looks like a controlled experiment and it does isolate one kind of variance: sampling. It cannot detect missing evidence - a stable answer generated from the wrong four chunks is perfectly repeatable - and the retrieved set can move between runs on its own (a rewrite step, ANN tie-breaking, fused ranks, changing filters), so a difference between runs still does not name the layer. Judge scores rank answers by how good they read, not by which layer failed, and length is a style signal: a short grounded answer and a short unevidenced one are indistinguishable by word count.

mcqs.question: A pricing assistant answers 'what does the Enterprise plan cost per seat?' with the annual figure for 5 of the 12 plans. The prices live in one 12-row table; the splitter emits one chunk per row and drops the header, so a chunk reads 'Enterprise | 60 | 4,800'. Retrieval returns the right rows for every one of those 5 questions. Where is the failure?
options: Chunk size: the 200-token budget is too small, so raise it to 800 and the whole table plus its header stays in one chunk, which restores the column names the model needs to read a row correctly.

Passage completeness at the row level: a row without its column labels is a bag of unattributed numbers, so the generator binds a value to the wrong column. Emit each row with its header and unit, or as labelled key-value lines, carry table and section metadata, and leave retrieval alone - it already returns the right rows.

Embedding quality: numbers and short strings embed poorly, so the top rows are near-interchangeable and the model receives them in an unstable order. Move to a model trained on tables and re-embed the table so the rows separate cleanly.

Arithmetic: the model should not be turning an annual figure into a per-seat answer at all, so give it a calculator tool and let it divide, instead of adding more context about how the table is laid out.
mcqs.explanation: High retrieval precision with a wrong value is a passage-level attribution failure, not a search failure: the rows arrive, and the chunk that arrives contains no header, no column name and no unit, so every number in it is ambiguous and the model resolves the ambiguity with the most plausible reading - annual for monthly. The fix has to put the label inside the passage, and small tables are cheap to emit as labelled lines (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.18059). The whole-table option only changes the odds if the table happens to stay under the budget, and a chunk that big costs specificity for every other question in the corpus. The strongest distractor is the embedding swap, because 'embeddings blur exact tokens' is true and re-embedding is visibly senior work - but that failure shows up as the wrong rows being returned, and here retrieval is perfect; no better vector can add a header that was never indexed. The calculator option misreads the symptom: 4,800 is printed in the table, so nothing needed computing, and a tool that divides a mislabelled number returns a confidently wrong number.

mcqs.question: Of 12,400 ingested PDFs, 31% produce no retrieval hits: their chunks never appear in the top 10 for questions they demonstrably answer, while the other 69% of the corpus behaves normally. A sample shows those files are scans with no text layer, and the parser returns an empty string for them. Where does the fix belong?
options: Chunking: split the scans into smaller windows so some non-empty fragments survive, and give the embedder less text per chunk so a partially recovered page can still match a question.

Parsing: OCR the documents that have no text layer, fix the table extraction that flattens rows, then re-chunk and re-embed - an empty string yields an empty chunk and a degenerate vector, which is why these files are invisible rather than mis-ranked.
Embedding: the model is weak on scanned layouts, so upgrade it and re-embed the corpus; the files will surface without re-parsing because the new vectors will represent that kind of page much better.
Ranking: raise k to 50 for the affected document types so chunks that were previously out of reach can enter the window; the rest of the corpus is healthy, which proves the index itself is intact.
mcqs.explanation: A failure that tracks a document class and a missing text layer is an extraction failure: nothing was ever produced for those pages, so no downstream stage has anything to act on, and the pipeline names it in the same words - a scanned PDF yields empty text (https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/grounding/overview). Detecting it is half the fix: track extracted characters per document and alert when a whole source class collapses to near zero, because the healthy 69% is what makes the failure silent. The strongest distractor is the embedding upgrade, because 'weak on scanned layouts' sounds like a real limitation and re-embedding is visibly senior work; but the embedder never receives characters - an empty chunk embeds to a degenerate vector, so the document is unreachable whichever model produces it. Smaller windows cannot recover text that does not exist, and raising k over rows that were never written returns nothing extra.

mcqs.question: A 50-page policy handbook (~30K tokens) is read by 400 employees who may all see every page, and it changes about once a month. The team plans parse, chunk, embed, HNSW and a reranker 'because that is how RAG is done', with no eval set. What design do you defend in review?
options: Put the handbook in the prompt behind a cached stable prefix, and add retrieval only for a named need: the corpus outgrows the window, visibility becomes per-user, or answers need per-claim attribution and freshness tighter than a deploy. Build the eval set either way.

Build the pipeline, but index the handbook as a single chunk so the architecture stays RAG-shaped without the cost of tuning retrieval quality or maintaining a splitter that can silently lose passages.

Build the pipeline, because attention over a 30K-token prompt is unreliable: models use the start and end of a long context well and the middle poorly, so retrieval is the safer design for a corpus this size.

Fine-tune on the handbook and skip both: 30K tokens is small enough to bake into the weights, and a monthly update makes the retraining cost trivial next to carrying the whole corpus on every request.
mcqs.explanation: The decision follows the needs, and none of the retrieval benefits is present: the corpus fits with room to spare, one audience reads all of it, and a monthly cadence is slower than most deploys - so a cached prefix costs one full pass and a fraction per call, with no recall to tune and no index to keep fresh (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/latency-optimization). The strongest distractor is the lost-in-the-middle argument, because the effect is real and it is the correct reason to structure a long prompt and then measure it; but here it is being used to assert that retrieval is 'safer' when neither design has been measured, and a top-5 retrieval over the same corpus also hands the model a short list it can mishandle. Switching mechanisms without an eval set just relocates the unknown. The single-chunk variant keeps every cost of a pipeline and removes its only benefit, and fine-tuning bakes in facts that change monthly and cannot be cited, scoped per user or corrected without a retrain.

mcqs.question: Queries containing an exact identifier ('ORA-01555', 'SKU 88-B') are 9% of support traffic, and for none of them is the correct runbook in the top 5: it usually sits around rank 40 of the 200 candidates that come back. Paraphrase questions work well. Which change targets the measured failure?
options: Add BM25 over the same chunks and fuse the two ranked lists with RRF before taking the head of the fused list: a rare literal token is exactly what lexical ranking weights, and rank fusion avoids pretending that a cosine score and a BM25 score are comparable.

Raise k from 5 to 50 for every query: the runbook is in the index and already in the candidate list, so a wider window will include it and the model can pick the right passage out of everything it receives.

Generate three paraphrases of each identifier query and search with all of them: a code that the embedder blurs under one phrasing may survive as a literal in another, so one of the three result lists should surface the runbook.

Tune the approximate index (ef_search, nprobe) until the runbook reaches the top 5: if approximate search only returns it at rank 40, the search parameters are leaving recall on the table and better ones can return it at rank 4.
mcqs.explanation: The evidence localizes the defect to the matching function, not to depth: the runbook is returned, it is just ranked by a similarity computed over a learned representation in which a synthetic identifier carries almost no signal, while paraphrases - the case the embedder is good at - are already healthy. BM25 weights a rare term heavily and RRF fuses positions without comparing incomparable scores; the fused shortlist then goes to a reranker if it is still noisy (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval). The strongest distractor is the ANN tuning, because 'approximate search' and 'never retrieved' sound like the same disease - here rank 40 of 200 proves the vector was returned, so the parameters are already doing their job and changing them only reshuffles a list that still ranks the code by meaning. Raising k to 50 spends ten times the prompt budget on every query to move a 9% case from invisible to buried, and paraphrasing a ticket number does not restore the literal: the rewrite re-embeds the same blur and triples the model calls.

mcqs.question: Finance asks: 'how many Enterprise accounts in EMEA churned last quarter, and what was their combined ARR at churn?' The CRM export is 40,000 rows, roughly 1.6M tokens. Someone proposes embedding each account as a chunk and letting the model count and sum from the top-20 retrieved accounts. A reviewed ARR model already exists in the warehouse. Which design answers the question?
options: Embed all 40,000 accounts and raise k to 500: at that depth the model sees enough rows to count them, and counting a sample of retrieved accounts is the only thing standing between it and the answer.

Query the warehouse through the governed ARR model for the count and the sum, return the value with the query and the rows it read, and keep retrieval for the narrative part, such as how the exit notes describe each churn.

Keep the vector search and add a calculator tool: the retrieved accounts are the relevant set, so the missing piece is arithmetic, and a sum tool over what the model retrieved closes the gap without touching the index.
Add a reranker over the 40,000 account chunks so the 20 accounts that matter for churn reliably surface first: better ordering is what turns a retrieved sample into a usable population.
mcqs.explanation: An aggregate is a scan over the set that matches a filter; retrieval returns a bounded top-k of passages chosen by similarity, so the model can only count what someone already put in front of it - 20 accounts out of 40,000 is a sample, and a sum over a sample is a number that looks exact. The warehouse model exists so that the count and the sum are computed by the thing that owns the definition (https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/about-metricflow), and the answer can carry the query and its rows as provenance. The strongest distractor is the calculator tool, because arithmetic is the visible symptom and 'give the model a tool' is a good reflex; but the tool would run over the retrieved set, so it computes the sum of the wrong population precisely and quickly, and retrieval would still be deciding which accounts exist. Long context fails on size here - 1.6M tokens does not fit - and k=500 of 40,000 rows is still a sample.

mcqs.question: Two answers to 'what is the refund window for Enterprise plans?' both cite retrieved chunk [2], and recall@5 on the eval set is 0.93. Answer A quotes the sentence it cites: 'up to 60 days, subject to the contract schedule'. Answer B states 'up to 45 days', a deadline that appears in no retrieved chunk. What is the correct reading?
options: Both are grounded, because each answer carries a citation into the retrieved set, and a recall@5 of 0.93 is the evidence that the passage supporting the answer was in the window when the answer was written.

A is grounded and B fails faithfulness: each claim in A is checkable against the passage it cites, while a citation proves only that something was retrieved. B's deadline is unsupported, which is a generation defect measured against the exact context passed, not an indexing one.
B is preferable, because it converts a 60-day maximum into the 45 days a customer actually gets: grounding only asks that an answer trace back into the corpus, and chunk [2] is corpus.

Both are equally suspect, because a wrong value after a healthy retrieval means the chunker cut the real deadline off the passage: re-chunk with overlap, re-index, and re-run the eval before judging either answer.
mcqs.explanation: Grounding is a relation between a claim and a specific retrieved passage, so it is checked claim by claim; retrieving something is not the same as grounding it, which is why retrieval quality and groundedness are scored separately (https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/grounding/overview). Here the evidence is present and one answer departs from it, so this is a faithfulness failure whose repair lives in the evidence format and the instruction to cite per claim, not in the index. The strongest distractor is 'both are grounded', because its premises are right - both cite, and recall is high - but a citation marks where the model claims its support comes from, not that the support exists; a citation is a pointer that an eval has to dereference. Re-chunking would be the right diagnosis only if a boundary had removed the 60-day sentence, and chunk [2] contains it.

mcqs.question: On 500 labelled queries the gold chunk is inside the top 100 for 94% of them but inside the top 5 for only 62%. The prompt takes 5 chunks, p95 latency has about 90ms of headroom, and the team already owns a cross-encoder. Which fix targets the measured gap?
options: Raise k to 100 and pass all 100 chunks: if the gold chunk is in the list the model can find it, and 100 passages of a few hundred tokens each are still small next to a 200K-token window.

Rerank the top-100 candidates with the cross-encoder, keep 6, and tune N against recall@5 and p95: the distance between 94% at rank 100 and 62% at rank 5 is an ordering defect, and a cross-encoder scores query and passage jointly instead of comparing two vectors.

Re-tune the approximate index (ef_search, nprobe) until the gold chunk reaches rank 5: if approximate search returns it at 40, better parameters can return it at 4 without adding any new model to the request path.
Add BM25 hybrid retrieval: exact-term matching is more precise than vector similarity, so the fused ranking will lift the gold chunk into the top 5 for the 32 points that are failing today.
mcqs.explanation: Two numbers from the same eval separate coverage from ordering: 94% inside the top 100 says candidate generation is fine, and 62% inside the top 5 says the ranking function is choosing the wrong five, which is exactly what a cross-encoder closes because it reads query and passage together; Anthropic's contextual-retrieval numbers have the same shape, with the reranker adding most of the gain over hybrid retrieval alone (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/contextual-retrieval). The strongest distractor is 'pass all 100', because in principle it does recover the missing 32 points; in practice it multiplies input tokens by twenty, buries the answer in the middle of a long context where models attend poorly, and leaves you unable to say which chunk was used. The ANN-parameter option mislabels an ordering problem as a recall problem - the chunk is already returned - and hybrid adds a lexical channel the evidence never asked for. Reranking 100 candidates is also 100 model calls per query, which is why N gets tuned and not defaulted.

mcqs.question: The eval is one LLM judge scoring each final answer 1-5 over 300 questions. After a chunker change the mean falls from 3.8 to 3.5 and nobody can say which layer regressed; the next release is blocked on that answer. What change makes the eval diagnostic?
options: Use a stronger judge and take three independent samples per answer, so measurement noise stops hiding the real difference between 3.8 and 3.5 before the next release is evaluated.

Record, per question, whether the gold chunk was in the retrieved set and whether each claim in the answer is supported by the exact context that was passed, then report the two rates separately alongside the chunk ids.
Grow the set to 3,000 questions: a larger sample narrows the confidence interval around each mean, and a real regression will separate from noise without changing what is being measured.
Have reviewers hand-label the 60 lowest-scoring answers after each change, so a human decides which kind of failure each one is and the team gets a taxonomy of mistakes to act on.
mcqs.explanation: One score for two layers cannot attribute anything: it collapses 'the passage never arrived' and 'the passage arrived and the answer ignored it' into the same number, which is the eval failure this pipeline names - only the final answer is measured, so a retrieval failure looks like a model failure. Two rates with chunk ids answer the blocked question directly: recall dropped means chunker or index; recall held while faithfulness dropped means prompt or evidence format (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/evals). The strongest distractor is the stronger judge with repeated samples, because it fixes a real problem - judge variance - but variance is not the blocker: a perfect, noise-free judge still returns one number for two layers, so 'which layer' stays unavailable. Scaling to 3,000 questions narrows the interval around the wrong metric, and hand-labelling the worst 60 yields a biased taxonomy with no rate attached.

mcqs.question: 1,800 policy pages are re-indexed nightly by upserting chunks whose ids are a hash of the chunk text. A policy replaced in March and a page deleted in April still answer as current in July, and nothing in the pipeline reports an error. What is the defect?
options: The nightly cadence: a full rebuild every night would drop the replaced and deleted content, so truncate the collection and rebuild the whole corpus in each run instead of upserting into the old one.

The keys and the delete path: hashing the chunk text turns every edit into an append, and nothing removes a deleted page, so derive ids from document id plus version, delete the previous set when a document changes, treat deletions as events, and prove it with a freshness eval.

The prompt: stamp each chunk with its source date and instruct the model to prefer the newest passage when two versions disagree, so a replaced policy loses to the current one at answer time without touching the index.

The embedder: the old model ranks stale passages as convincingly as fresh ones because its space does not encode recency, so upgrading to a newer embedding model is what lets current pages win the ranking.
mcqs.explanation: The index is a cache of the source of truth, so an edit has to become a replacement and a deletion has to become an event. Neither exists here: hashing the text makes new text a new key while the old keys stay, and nothing in the pipeline can express 'this page is gone' (https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/grounding/overview). Chunk ids derived from document id plus version, a delete-then-write per document, and a freshness eval with one edited and one deleted question make the regression fail in CI instead of in July. The strongest distractor is the prompt option, because dating chunks is a real practice and it sounds like a cheap fix; but a date is a signal, not an enforcement - the superseded chunk is still served and still ranked, 'prefer the newest' is an instruction the model may ignore, and the deleted page must not be in the collection at all. A nightly full rebuild re-pays for the entire corpus to fix a problem that change events fix in the one affected document, and an embedding upgrade addresses a ranking cause that has nothing to do with why a deleted file answers.

mcqs.question: A 40-page handbook (~24K tokens) is pasted as a cached prefix in the system prompt; answers are fast and they were correct on day one. Another team updates the handbook every Thursday. Since the switch, replies quote last quarter's limits, and nobody has touched the prompt. What is the actual fault?
options: The cache expiry: provider caches are short-lived, so weekly edits cannot persist and the model falls back to what it absorbed in training for anything the window no longer holds reliably.

The prefix is a copy that nothing rebuilds: change detection and invalidation are missing, so wire source events or an updated_at poll to regenerate the prefix, key the cache on a content hash, and add an eval question whose answer changed last week.

The long-context design: switching to RAG fixes this, because a retrieval index is rebuilt from the source when documents change and does not carry a stale copy of the handbook the way a prompt prefix does.

The instruction: with the whole handbook already in the window there is nothing to retrieve, so tell the model to prefer the most recent limits it can see and lower the temperature so it stops improvising.
mcqs.explanation: Staleness is a property of the copy, not of the mechanism holding it: a prompt prefix is a copy of the handbook exactly as an index is, and the missing piece in both designs is the path from 'the source changed' to 'the copy changed' - so the repair is change detection, regeneration and invalidation, proven by a question whose expected answer moved last week (https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/latency-optimization). The strongest distractor is 'switch to RAG', because it sounds like the senior answer in a retrieval area and it correctly describes what a well-run index does; but RAG does not add change detection on its own - a pipeline fed by the same process that never told anyone about the Thursday edit is stale in exactly the same way, with an extra embedder, an extra hop and a new recall failure mode. Cache expiry explains a cost spike, not outdated content, since an expired cache is recomputed from the same stale prefix. The instruction option asks the model to repair data that is wrong before the model sees it, and nothing in the window says which limit is the older one.

mcqs.question: A claims assistant must answer from 300K internal case files that change daily, with per-team visibility and a citation on every answer. A vendor proposes fine-tuning on the files so the knowledge sits in the weights and the retrieval hop disappears. Which objection is decisive?
options: Cost: fine-tuning on 300K files is too expensive and too slow to refresh, so the plan becomes reasonable if it trains on the 5,000 most-asked cases instead of the whole corpus.

The three requirements are query-time properties: daily changes need incremental writes, per-team visibility needs a filter evaluated per requester, and a citation needs a source pointer - weights give none of them, while retrieval plus ACL at query time gives all three.

Quality: fine-tuning always degrades the base model's general ability, so knowledge should never be trained into weights and the retrieval hop has to stay regardless of cost, freshness or permissions.
Cadence: the only real objection is that daily retraining is impractical, so a weekly retrain with a pinned model version is an acceptable trade for removing the retrieval hop from the request path.
mcqs.explanation: The decisive test is whether the mechanism can even express the requirement: weights cannot be updated incrementally (every change is a training run), cannot be filtered per user (the file you must not see sits in the same model as the one you may), and cannot point at the paragraph an answer came from - so fine-tuning bakes in facts that have to stay addressable, revocable and attributable, which is what retrieval plus access control at query time provides (https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/). The strongest distractor is the weekly-retrain compromise, because it engages the mechanism and appears to answer the cadence problem that was actually raised; but cadence was the least of the three, and a weekly model still cannot withhold one team's files from another team or say which file it used. Training on the most-asked 5,000 cases answers a different question, since the long tail is why the corpus exists, and 'fine-tuning always hurts' reaches the right conclusion by a false route.

mcqs.question: A support assistant finds the right policy document for 95% of questions, yet answers keep stating a rule without the exception that follows it: the condition ends one chunk and the list it qualifies starts the next. Chunks are 512 tokens, split on a fixed character count, with no overlap. Which diagnosis and next step fit the evidence?
options: The embedding model is the weak link: 0.95 document recall with poor answers means the vectors barely separate the relevant sentences, so upgrade the model and re-embed the corpus.

Passage completeness: fixed-size splitting cut the condition away from the list it qualifies, so the top-k chunks are on topic but individually unable to support the answer. Split on document structure, keep section and position metadata, add overlap only where facts cross boundaries, and re-run recall plus faithfulness on boundary-spanning questions.
Retrieval depth: raise top-k from 5 to 20 so the neighbouring passage enters the window, because more retrieved context can only help the generator.
Specificity: shrink chunks to about 100 tokens so each retrieved passage is tighter and the model is not distracted by unrelated sentences.
mcqs.explanation: Document-level recall near the ceiling with low answer faithfulness localizes the failure to the passage, not the search: the evidence needed to answer is being cut apart at the boundary, so the fix is structural splitting with section and position metadata, plus an eval made of questions whose evidence spans two chunks (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.18059). The embedding-swap option is the strongest distractor because upgrading the model is a real senior move and re-embedding is real work, but a high document recall says the vectors are already putting the right document in the window; the missing sentence is in a different chunk, which no better vector can pull into the passage that was cut. Raising top-k masks the symptom only if the neighbouring chunk happens to carry the rest of the fact and survive ranking, while it spends prompt budget and adds distractor text; shrinking chunks moves the same boundary faster and loses definitions, which is the opposite of the measured failure.

mcqs.question: A team adds HyDE to support search: a generated hypothetical answer is embedded and its nearest real chunks are retrieved. The PR also proposes passing that generated answer to the generator as context. Over the eval set, recall@10 goes from 0.71 to 0.80 while faithfulness drops from 0.88 to 0.79. Which reading and change are right?
options: Ship it: recall@10 is the metric that decides retrieval quality, and the generated text is only extra context that the generator is free to ignore.
Drop query rewriting entirely: a drop in faithfulness proves that generated queries are unsound in every case.

Use the generated text as a retrieval probe only, never as evidence: keep the original query alongside for audit, gate the rewrite to the query types where the baseline fails (conversational, underspecified, vocabulary mismatch), and require grounded-answer quality and latency to hold before shipping.
Keep the design as is but add an instruction telling the model to ignore any claim that is not present in the retrieved chunks.
mcqs.explanation: A rewrite is a retrieval instrument, not a source: HyDE retrieves real documents near a hypothetical answer, and feeding that synthetic text to the generator as evidence invites invented details to be answered and cited, which is exactly what the faithfulness drop measures (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10496, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07678). Keeping the original query preserves comparison and audit, and gating the technique to the query shapes where the baseline fails is how the gain is paid for by the extra model call. The strongest distractor is "ship it", because its premise is right — recall@k is the retrieval metric — but it stops one measurement too early: recall only says the right chunk arrived, not that the answer is grounded in it, and a generated paragraph reads to the model like any other policy statement. Dropping the technique overcorrects a subset win into a total loss, and the ignore-what-is-not-retrieved instruction has no signal to act on, since nothing in the context marks which sentences are synthetic.

mcqs.question: Tail-query recall is poor, so you plan to move from embedding model v1 (768 dimensions, cosine) to v2 (1024 dimensions, dot product). The index holds 40M chunks and serves live traffic. Which migration plan is correct?
options: Re-embed the corpus in place, oldest documents first, into a 1024-dimension index; cosine and dot product converge once the vectors are normalized.
Backfill only the chunks that fail retrieval today and zero-pad the v1 vectors to 1024 dimensions so both models can share one index while the tail improves.
Keep the exact flat index and switch the metric to L2: with no approximation error, the model and metric choices stop affecting which chunks come back.

Treat it as a rebuild under a new contract: build a shadow v2 index, dual-write new and updated documents to both, compare recall@k and p95 latency on production-shaped queries, then cut over atomically with a rollback path — old and new vectors are never mixed in one index.
mcqs.explanation: Model, dimension, preprocessing, metric and chunking are all part of the vector contract, so changing the model is a rebuild, and the cutover is an experiment with a shadow index plus production-shaped queries rather than a switch flipped on live traffic; if the shadow index needs approximate search, HNSW's memory-and-effort parameters get tuned against those same queries (https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320, https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes). The strongest distractor is the in-place re-embed, because it avoids operating two indexes and sounds incremental, but vectors from two models live in different spaces with different dimensions: there is no meaningful distance between a v1 vector and a v2 vector, so a mixed index returns noise, and the metric change is an assumption in that option rather than something verified. Zero-padding preserves the incomparability while skipping the tail queries that motivated the change, and the flat-index option confuses exactness inside one space with compatibility between two: exact search returns the true nearest v1 neighbours, which are precisely the rankings that are failing.

scenarios.prompt: Users report that the documentation assistant cites the right document but the wrong sentence, and answers change when the same question is asked twice with slightly different wording.

code.code:
chunks = split_by_chars(doc, size=1500)
results = vector_store.search(embed(query), k=4)

scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Prediction.** The report contains two different failures, and this code explains both.

*Right document, wrong sentence.* `split_by_chars(doc, size=1500)` emits spans that know nothing about sentences: a boundary can land inside a clause, between a heading and its paragraph, or after the first row of a table. The hit that comes back carries no offsets and no section, so the only fact the system has is 'this text came from doc 42'. Anything that highlights a sentence is therefore reconstructing a location - the first sentence of the chunk, the longest sentence, or the sentence that matches the query terms - and the reconstruction is wrong exactly when the chunk does not begin at the sentence that answers. The asymmetry users describe is the giveaway: the document is right because the document is the only part that was recorded.

*Answer changes with slightly different wording.* At 1500 characters a chunk holds roughly 350-400 tokens, which in documentation is several near-related sections; the embedding is an average of those topics. Rephrase the question and several candidates reorder inside the top 4. With `k=4` from a single retriever, slots 3 and 4 are near-ties decided by wording, so the generator answers from a partly different set of passages and produces a different, individually plausible answer.

**What I would measure before changing either.** Log `chunk_id` per request for a week and diff the sets for paraphrase pairs. If the failing questions retrieve different chunks, the instability is retrieval and the fix is ranking; if the sets are identical and the text still moves, it is sampling and the conversation moves to the prompt. Without that split, both complaints get treated as one and one of them is fixed twice.

**Defects, in impact order.**

1. **Boundaries are characters, not structure.** Headings, list items and table rows are the units that carry meaning in documentation; a fixed window cuts them apart and produces passages that are on topic but incomplete.
2. **No provenance.** The chunk record has to carry `doc_id`, `section_path`, `start`, `end`, `page` and a version. With offsets the citation is the span the model actually read, and the UI can assert `raw.slice(start, end) === chunk.text` before it highlights anything.
3. **No overlap where facts cross.** Overlap is not a default for every chunk - it doubles storage and returns near-duplicates. It is worth adding only across boundaries where a definition and its exception, or a table header and its rows, cannot be kept together.
4. **One retriever, k=4, no second stage.** Paraphrase sensitivity and exact-term misses have the same practical remedy: BM25 plus vectors fused with RRF, then a reranker over the shortlist.
5. **No eval.** 'Cites the wrong sentence' is not measurable today, because nothing states what the right sentence is.

**The change I would ship.**

- Chunk by structure: split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, targeting 300-500 tokens, and never emit a chunk without its heading path. Keep a table with its header row, either as a whole table or as rows that repeat the labels.
- Record provenance: `chunk_id = doc_id@version#ordinal`, plus `section_path`, `start`, `end`, `page`, `source_updated_at`. The id is stable enough to cache and versioned enough that an edit replaces instead of appending.
- Rank in two stages: BM25 and vector top-50 each, fused with RRF, then a cross-encoder keeps 5-6 for the prompt. That is the direct answer to paraphrase sensitivity, because two wordings that tie in vector space are separated by a model that reads query and passage together.
- Require the answer to quote the sentence it relies on, and validate that the quote falls inside a retrieved span before rendering. A citation the UI cannot dereference is decoration.

**Acceptance.** Span-level recall@5 (is the gold span inside one of the five chunks) and citation precision (does the quoted span contain the answering sentence), reported per question type; plus a paraphrase-pair check that the same question in two wordings returns the same chunk ids. Ship when the ids are stable and both rates beat the current baseline - and only then look at generation.
rubric: Separates the two symptoms: no offsets or section means the highlighted sentence is reconstructed (provenance), while 350-400 token mixed-topic chunks with k=4 explain wording sensitivity (ordering) - and does not fold both into 'chunking'.
Says how to tell them apart with evidence: log chunk ids per request, diff the sets for paraphrase pairs, and build an eval with gold spans rather than gold documents.
Fixes provenance concretely: doc id + version + ordinal ids, section path, start/end offsets, and citations the UI verifies against the source text.
Fixes ranking with a measured second stage - BM25 plus vector fused by rank, then a reranked shortlist, k kept small - instead of enlarging the prompt.
Names an acceptance test: span-level recall@5 plus citation precision, and a paraphrase-pair check that identical questions return identical chunk ids.

scenarios.prompt: The legal team wants to ask questions about 40 structured contracts with amounts, dates and parties. They ask for a vector store over the exported PDFs.

code.code:
docs = [export_pdf(c) for c in contracts]
index = build_vector_index(docs)

scenarios.modelAnswer:
**First, read the request as a symptom.** The team asks for a vector store because that is the pattern they have heard of, but the questions they describe - amounts, dates, parties - are field lookups. Retrieval answers with prose that mentions a number; a query answers with the number. Before building anything I would pull their last two weeks of real questions and sort them into three buckets:

- **field lookups** - 'what is the liability cap in the Acme MSA', 'when does contract 17 expire';
- **filters and aggregates** - 'which contracts renew in Q1', 'total value by counterparty';
- **narrative** - 'how is force majeure worded here', 'which of these indemnities is the most aggressive'.

If the first two buckets dominate, a vector store over exported PDFs is the wrong primary index, and I would say so with those counts.

**Why the PDF index fails on the first two buckets.**

1. The value has to survive parsing. An exported PDF loses column alignment, and a fee schedule becomes a line of digits - the pipeline's own first failure mode.
2. Embeddings represent meaning, not strings: 'EUR 1,200,000' and 'EUR 210,000' sit close in vector space because both are money, so the ranking is content to return the wrong clause.
3. Retrieval returns k passages; it cannot enumerate a filtered set. 'Which contracts renew in Q1' becomes 'which of the eight passages I happened to retrieve renew in Q1'.
4. Sums, comparisons and date arithmetic are done by the model in its head over prose, which is precisely where unsupported numbers come from.

**The design I would defend.**

1. **Extract a record per contract**: parties (legal name, role), dates (effective, expiry, notice), amounts (fee, cap, currency, period) and obligations, each with a pointer to page and clause. Model extraction is fine; what makes it trustworthy is that every field stores its source clause text and a confidence, and low-confidence amounts go to a review queue. A wrong cap in a legal assistant is worse than 'not found'.
2. **Store it relationally.** Contracts, parties, clauses and obligations as tables; money as `numeric` with a currency column; every row carrying `contract_id`, `clause_ref`, `page`, `source_sha`. At 40 contracts, re-extraction on change is cheap.
3. **Answer values through a tool, not through text.** Expose a small read-only query tool with a validated argument shape; the answer returns the value plus the clause citation. The model never restates a number it read out of a PDF it parsed itself.
4. **Keep retrieval for the narrative bucket, at clause granularity.** One chunk per clause, with contract id and clause number as metadata, answers 'how is this worded' well and gives a precise citation. Indexing whole PDFs is what makes citations vague and retrieval noisy.
5. **Say 'not specified' out loud.** Many questions will land on a contract that is silent on the point, and that has to be an allowed answer or the model will fill the gap.

**Acceptance.** Sixty questions with known answers: exact match on every value, a citation that opens the right page and clause, and a set of 'silent contract' cases whose expected answer is 'not specified'. If value accuracy misses, the fix is extraction quality and review, not a better embedder.

**What I tell the legal team.** The PDFs stay the evidence of record and every answer links back to the clause. What changes is that the values live in a queryable model, because a question about a number deserves a query and a question about wording deserves retrieval - one assistant can do both, with the query as the first-class path.
rubric: Reframes the request before building: asks what shape the questions have, and states that field lookups and aggregates are cases where a query or a governed model beats a vector store.

Explains the mechanism, not just the preference: embeddings blur exact values, retrieval cannot enumerate a filtered population, and arithmetic over retrieved prose is where unsupported numbers come from.
Proposes the concrete model: extracted contract/party/clause/obligation records with page and clause provenance, money stored with currency, and a review path for extracted amounts.
Keeps retention for the part it is good at - clause-level chunks for 'how is this worded' and cross-contract narrative - instead of rejecting retrieval outright.
Defines acceptance: exact-match on values, citations to page and clause, and 'silent contract' cases where the correct answer is 'not specified'.

scenarios.prompt: A knowledge assistant answers well in demos but after a month cites policies that were replaced. The index is rebuilt manually every quarter.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
**Prediction.** Two shapes, and this code produces both.

*For the rest of the quarter:* correct answers, which is why the demo looked good - the demo ran shortly after a rebuild. Then the policy team replaces a policy, the index still holds the old text, and the assistant cites a document that no longer exists on the wiki and states a rule that was repealed. Nobody sees an error, because a stale chunk is a perfectly valid chunk.

*At the next rebuild:* one of two things, and both are bad. If `index.build()` appends into the existing collection, the superseded text and the new text both answer, so one question can return last quarter's rule next to this quarter's. If it truncates and rebuilds, there is a window with no index at all, and the entire corpus is re-parsed and re-embedded to publish a handful of edits.

**The code, line by line.**

- `rebuild()` is the only path from source to index and a human triggers it. There is no change capture, so freshness is a calendar property instead of a property of the source.
- It builds unconditionally: no deletes, no versioned ids, no diff. Whatever the chunk ids are, nothing expresses 'this document changed' or 'this document is gone'.
- No metadata: no `source_updated_at`, no `valid_until`, so an answer cannot say 'as of' and a reviewer cannot tell which version was used.
- No monitoring: no index lag, no alert, no eval. A user discovers the failure.
- A full rebuild is used for content, which is the case it is not for - full rebuilds are for chunker, embedder, metric or schema changes, where every vector must be recomputed anyway.

**The loop that replaces it.**

1. **Capture changes at the source.** The wiki emits events or exposes `updated_at`; poll it on a schedule if events are unavailable, and include deletions and moves, not just edits and creates.
2. **Re-index one document.** Derive ids as `policy/{doc_id}@{version}/{ordinal}`, delete that document's previous ids, write the new set, and do both in one operation so a reader never sees the document missing or doubled.
3. **Carry validity into the chunk.** `source_updated_at` always, `valid_until` where the source has an expiry, so the prompt can say 'as of 12 March' and the UI can show it.
4. **Treat deletion as an event with the same priority as an edit.** This is the classic miss: inserts get wired, deletes do not, and a repealed policy keeps answering for weeks.
5. **Let 'not in the index yet' be a valid answer.** Otherwise the model fills the gap from the nearest stale passage and sounds confident.
6. **Measure the lag.** Record time from source change to searchable, alert when it exceeds the promise (say 15 minutes), and keep it on a dashboard. 'Never stale' is not achievable; 'stale by at most X' is.

**Proving it.** Three eval questions on every deploy: one whose answer changed last week, one whose answer was deleted, one whose answer exists only in the source. Add an assertion that no superseded document id can appear in a citation. If answers are cached downstream, invalidate on index write too - the cache sits after the index, and refreshing one does not refresh the other.

**What I keep the full rebuild for.** Changing the chunker, the embedding model or the metadata schema, because then every vector is invalid. That migration is a shadow index with dual writes, a comparison on production-shaped queries, and a cutover with a rollback path - not a `rebuild()` on a Friday.
rubric: Diagnoses both layers at once: quarterly cadence explains the month-long staleness, and an append-only build explains old and new text answering side by side - including the truncate variant that empties the index during a rebuild.
Separates content freshness from a full rebuild: full rebuilds are reserved for chunker, embedding model or schema changes; content updates are incremental, keyed to change events.
Specifies the mechanics: versioned chunk ids from document id plus version, delete-then-write per document, deletions as change events, and source_updated_at/valid_until in the metadata.
Makes missing evidence legitimate - 'not in the index yet' must be answerable as such - and handles the cache downstream of the index.

Defines proof and the SLA: three freshness eval questions (changed, deleted, source-only), a superseded-citation assertion, and a measured index lag with an alert threshold instead of a promise of never stale.

scenarios.prompt: This retrieval helper answers support questions from an internal wiki. The wiki is re-indexed every night and some pages are restricted to managers. Review the code and say what breaks in production.
rubric: Identifies the unused `user` parameter as an authorization defect enforced at query time - top-k must be k permitted chunks - and rejects 'filter after retrieval' and 'instruct the model to ignore' as fixes.
Names the second-order risk rather than only the disclosure: ingested wiki text is untrusted input, so restricted content and injected instructions can reach the wrong requester's context.
Identifies staleness as a missing delete/version path (edits append, deletions never remove), separate from whether a nightly cadence is acceptable, and makes 'no evidence' a legitimate outcome.
Shows a fix where the filter, the abstention branch and the returned source ids are visible, and explains what each one buys.
Proposes retrieval-side tests for the forbidden, stale/deleted, injected and missing cases, scored separately from generation.

scenarios.prompt: This chunker indexes a 4,000-page internal handbook that is re-indexed nightly. Product reports that replies often state a rule without the exception attached to it, and QA reports that "view source" highlights land on the wrong paragraph. Retrieval evaluation shows document recall@5 of 0.94 with answer faithfulness of 0.55. Predict what users will experience, name the defects in this code, and refactor it into a structural chunker with usable provenance. Assume `raw` is the full document text and that a table or a long list can arrive as a single paragraph.
rubric: Predicts the user-visible failure precisely: document recall is high, so retrieval is on topic, but the passage omits the exception because the condition and the list it qualifies were cut apart — not that the model ignored available text.

Finds the offset defects: `start` never advances by the separator and the mid-loop `end` is the chunk length rather than `start + text.length`, so citations and highlights drift; proposes an assert that `raw.slice(start, end)` equals the chunk text.

Identifies lost structure: `section` is hardcoded `"unknown"`, so heading context and section filters are gone; rebuilds sections before chunking and carries section plus document version as metadata.

Handles oversize blocks and boundaries: a table or long list pasted as one paragraph is emitted whole, so it is split on rows or sentences; overlap is modest and targeted, and hierarchical summaries are named for document-level context.

States the acceptance test and the migration: a boundary-spanning eval on recall and faithfulness, length distribution checks, and a re-index with versioned chunk ids so edited or deleted documents leave no stale passages.
